title: Sustained-QPS microbatch governor with KV snapshot compaction and graded GPU headroom
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description:
Problem: In steady high-QPS workloads (>10k tokens/s per tenant) we observe repeated microburst/quiet cycles that lead to 2 failure modes: (1) frequent tiny microbatches that raise per-token overhead and increase cost, and (2) KV cache churn + GPU memory fragmentation that causes transient OOMs and p95 latency spikes. Current admission heuristics react too quickly to short-term windows and cause oscillation instead of graceful degradation.

Proposed solution summary: Implement a Sustained-QPS Microbatch Governor that (A) tracks QPS and sequence-length distributions using a sliding window with hysteresis, (B) periodically takes lightweight KV snapshots to guide compaction decisions instead of relying on instantaneous eviction pressure, and (C) reserves a small GPU headroom pool with graded backpressure (soft vs hard) to avoid catastrophic OOMs while preserving throughput for high-priority tenants. The governor will emit observability signals and support runtime flags for canary rollout.

Key design points:
- Windowing and hysteresis: maintain two windows (short: 1s, long: 60s) and only change microbatch thresholds when long-window metrics cross thresholds for N windows to avoid flip-flopping.
- KV snapshot compaction: take an approximate LRU snapshot of hot keys at low frequency (30s) to guide compaction tiers (hot,warm,cold) rather than immediately evicting on pressure. Snapshot uses per-key access counts and recent token delta.
- Graded GPU headroom pool: maintain a tenant-agnostic reserved pool (configurable tokens/MB) that is used when an admission bump would exceed available memory; soft backpressure will delay low-priority requests briefly, hard backpressure rejects requests with a structured Retry-After and alternative route.
- Tenant priority and fairness: integrate with existing priority slots to ensure SLO-critical tenants are favored when headroom is scarce.
- Fallbacks: when headroom exhausted, automatically fallback to smaller compatible model variant (if configured) and log rollback events.

Success metrics:
- Reduce p95 generation latency spikes by 40% under sustained high-QPS load in lab testing.
- Reduce OOM incidents on serving fleet by 90% for affected capacity classes.
- Maintain throughput within 10% of baseline and reduce microbatch variance (stddev of batch size) by 30%.

Operational and rollout plan:
1) Implement feature-flagged runtime in canary region with sampling enabled (small percent of requests).
2) Run synthetic sustained-QPS tests using replay harness and real traffic shadowing for 48h.
3) Monitor dashboards: p50/p95 latency, KV hitrate, eviction rate, GPU free memory, batch size distribution.
4) If canary stable for 72h with metric improvements, rollout to 10% of capacity, then 50% and full.

Artifacts and links:
- Design doc (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RW/Sustained-QPS+Microbatch+Governor
- Load test harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks/pulls/218
- PR (initial impl): https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1543
- Observability dashboard (Grafana): https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/rvGqQ/microbatch-governor-canary

Risks:
- Snapshot frequency tuning may accidentally increase CPU overhead; we will start conservative (30s) and adjust.
- Incorrect tenant priority configuration could starve lower tiers; integration tests required.
- Interaction with KV persistent policies (compaction/replication) needs validation with infra team.

Next steps:
- Finalize snapshot representation and compaction tiers (action: Marco, due 2026-02-27).
- Prototype headroom reservation allocator and simple soft-backpressure hook (action: infra pairing, due 2026-03-06).
- Create canary runbook and rollback criteria (action: SRE, due 2026-03-12).
